text: A household decides what did not happen, and then requires everyone in it to live by that decision. The widow of a nobleman has a child by a servant; when the in-laws find out, the man and the infant are put outside the gate and the matter is treated as closed. Shin Sang-ok is interested in the long afterward rather than the scandal: the boy grows up, the mother holds to a version of her life that costs her a son to maintain. No one raises a voice. In 101 minutes the film watches a rule do its work, never argued and never defended, enforced at the pace of ordinary days by relatives who share their meals. It took the Grand Bell for Best Film in 1963, an official prize for a picture whose subject is the cost of correct conduct.

Fourteen years away, and the street is still standing; that turns out to be the harder outcome. A man who spent those years in Japan comes back to the Seoul neighborhood that raised him, and Im Kwon-taek keeps him walking it — the shopfronts, the people who stayed, the arithmetic of who married whom — well past the point where the plot would ordinarily hand him a fight. What waits for him is not an enemy but an account. He is asked, by everyone he greets, to square the neighborhood he carried around for fourteen years with the one that went on without him. 112 minutes, most of them at street level. The Baeksang for Best Film went to it, a domestic verdict on a story that never leaves a few blocks.

At the wake, the dead man's sister is working the room with insurance policies. Park Cheol-su sets a comedy inside a Confucian funeral in a village where everyone must be fed, seated and asked after: the eldest son back from directing films, the daughter who gave her parents grief and now cannot stop crying, the third son in from America, rehearsing hymns for rites that were not built to accommodate them. The house fills. The observances proceed on their own schedule whether or not the children are equal to them, and mourning gets crowded out by reunion, gossip, obligation and food. None of the comedy is at anyone's expense. It comes from the arithmetic of a small place, where the death of one old man is also the largest gathering the village will hold, and the living have business with each other.

In 1800 a court official is assigned to edit the archive of a dead king, and dies before the job is done. Park Chong-won builds his mystery out of paperwork: which sentences enter the permanent record of Yeongjo's reign, who decides, and what a faction will do to keep a volume from being bound. The quarrel underneath is constitutional — power gathered in the king, or spread among his ministers — and neither side can say so plainly, so it proceeds by appointment, precedent and a death that has to be explained as something else. 126 minutes of men who cannot draw swords doing damage with documents instead. The Grand Bell for Best Film went to it in 1995. Its idea of suspense is that an archive is an instrument of power, and everyone in the room knows it.

He hires her, and everything after that has to be built on top of the transaction. The man left Argentina for the United States years ago and is back only because business required it; Paula's family has a long name and no money, which makes her available for hire in a way nobody involved will say out loud. Fernando Ayala keeps the imbalance in the frame instead of dissolving it in romance: the wage, the errands, the fact that one of these two can leave the country whenever he likes and the other cannot. A hundred minutes, 1963, the Silver Condor for Best Film. Feeling arrives anyway, as it does. It does not cancel the arithmetic underneath it; it only makes the arithmetic harder to keep looking at.

The family moves twice, in opposite directions, and neither move helps. A father on the edge of Buenos Aires cannot keep the household afloat, so he takes it back to the country he came from, where his own father and brother are out of work too, and then back to the city again. Tristán Bauer gives the round trip two hours, long enough for it to stop reading as a plot and start reading as a condition. Two children are carried through it, which changes the price of every decision made above their heads. Argentina in 1991 enters the film as work and prices rather than as politics; the Silver Condor for Best Film went to it. There is no correct version of the choice these adults keep making. There is only the version they can afford that week.

A doctor takes a post on an island where her patients are kept apart from everyone else, and the film stays out there with her for all 88 of its minutes. She is a woman practicing medicine in Japan in 1940, in a place the mainland has arranged not to think about, and the work is mostly ordinary work: examinations, records, the persuasion required to bring one more patient in. Shirō Toyoda films the colony as a settlement rather than a subject, people with names, routines, weather. Kinema Junpo gave it the year's best film. What lasts is the plain register: separation practiced as procedure, recorded while it was simply how things were done, by a filmmaker who took the doctor's patience to be the thing worth the running time.

The woman in this documentary is named Agneta, and so is the director. Jean is hurt in a freak accident, and the 79 minutes that follow belong to the part that comes after the emergency: a body that works differently now, a household built for the old one, two people obliged to work out what they are to each other on the far side of it. Recovery is not treated as a story with a shape. It is kept at the level of days, appointments, rooms, the labor of getting from morning to evening. Sweden's Guldbagge for best film went to it, which puts a documentary of household difficulty where a national cinema usually puts its showpiece. Whatever distance a camera is meant to supply, this one does not appear to have had any of it.

A woman with a company to run keeps dreaming, and at some point she drives to the coast to have it out with the dreams. Kim Soo-yong sets her down in a fishing village where nothing she is good at applies — no office, no staff, no one who has heard of her — and then lets the trip stop being hers to direct. The film is filed as thriller and mystery and earns both. The frightening part is structural: how few steps it takes to move a person with money and a title into a place where neither counts for anything, and how unremarkable the people doing the moving are. 95 minutes, 1977, the Baeksang for Best Film. The dreams are not her problem. They are the part of her that already knows where she is going.

In 1949 an Argentine studio spent ninety-two minutes on the life of a poet. That is an unusual place to put a production's money, and it sets a problem no budget solves: the work at the center of such a life happens silently, at a desk. Whatever Luis César Amadori found to put on screen had to stand in for that. The film is titled with the poet's name and nothing more, which suggests the name was expected to bring an audience in by itself, true of a writer in one country and almost nowhere else. The Silver Condor for Best Film followed. Watching it now is partly watching what a national cinema of the 1940s thought a poet was for, and how confidently it assumed the people in the seats had read him.

The story is told backward, so Federico's choices are watched by someone who already knows what came of them. He is one of several children of a mother raising them alone, and he works in a neighborhood bar, a job that keeps him in company he would not otherwise be keeping. Claudio is part of that company, and what he offers is an easier life. Mario Soffici spends 115 minutes on something that is less a fall than a series of small subtractions: an evening not spent at home, a friend not answered, a set of obligations allowed to lapse. The Silver Condor for Best Film went to it in 1954. Nothing Federico gains comes out of a stranger's pocket. It all comes out of the people who were already counting on him.

Ten minutes long, and it took the Canadian Screen Award for Best Motion Picture. The story is Tsimshian: an old medicine man who has lost his sight, a loon, and the white marking the bird wears on its neck as a result of what passes between them. At that length a legend has to move the way legends move, no psychology, no preparation, one event pressing straight onto the next, and a 1948 English-language production had to find pictures for something that had been kept in speech. The distance between those two things is the film. Nothing in it is explained twice. What a viewer registers now, apart from the images, is the question of who is telling this and to whom. Ten minutes leaves no room to soften anything.
